newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. stocks seen up after CPI.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. stocks seen up after CPI.

text.p: U.S. stocks were seen opening higher on Wednesday after the release of a lower-than-expected January Consumer Price Index, analysts said.
--GUY TRUICKO, EQUITY PORTFOLIO MANAGER AT UNITY MANAGEMENT:
-- "It should be positive today, but the market was up 78 points yesterday so it's kind of hard to say how much of this already in there. But it certainly provides a good backdrop."

The Labor Department reported that the January CPI rose 0.1 percent, after a 0.3 percent rise in December. Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the index rose 0.1 percent in January after rising a revised 0.2 percent in December.
Wall Street economists had expected the CPI to rise 0.3 percent in January, and post an 0.2 percent rise excluding food and energy items.
-- PHIL ORLANDO, CHIEF INVESTMENT OFFICER OF VALUE LINE'S ASSET MANAGEMENT DIVISION
-- "Bonds will rally. Stocks will soar, led by technology."

-- "The nominal number is two-tenths less than expected, and the core number is half of what was expected. This provides us with solid confirmation for last Friday's PPI number. There are no inflationary pressures in the economy. I continue to forecast no change in policy at the March 25 FOMC meeting."
-- LARRY WACHTEL, ANALYST AT PRUDENTIAL SECURITIES:
-- Said the data was "favorable" but might not produce a major boost to stocks. "We already know that that inflationary pressures are minimal. This is not a revelation."

-- "The inflation figures are below expectations, but they are offset a bit by the trade figures. The deficit is wider than expected. The problem is that Europe is in such sluggish condition. If your major markets are sluggish you won't get a lot of exports. It has inflationary conotations. That's why it offsets the CPI number to a certain degree."
The Commerce Department reported the international trade deficit in December expanded to $10.29 billion from a revised $7.94 bilion in November. Economists had expected an increase to $9.9 billion.
